did_you_know.text: Did you know? The prophet Nathan did not come to David on his own initiative: Scripture says that the LORD sent him to rebuke the king through a parable.
Did you know? The poor man’s ewe lamb is described almost like a member of the family: it ate his food, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, and grew up with his children.
Did you know? David pronounced two punishments on the rich man in the parable: death and repayment of four times the value of the lamb, because he had shown no pity to the poor man.
Did you know? The turning point in Nathan’s rebuke is the short sentence: “You are the man!” David realizes that the parable is not about a stranger, but about his own actions.

Did you know? Nathan accused David of having Uriah the Hittite killed by the sword of the Ammonites, even though David was held responsible because he had caused Uriah to be placed in the most dangerous part of the battle.

Did you know? Because of David’s sin, Nathan announced that the sword would never depart from David’s household. This punishment matched David’s actions, which had brought about Uriah’s death by the sword.

Did you know? David confessed his sin in a short, direct statement: “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan replied that the LORD had taken away his sin, but announced that the son who had been born would die.

Did you know? The child died on the seventh day. David’s servants were afraid to tell him, because they thought that if he had reacted this way while the child was alive, he might harm himself after the child’s death.
Did you know? David explained that after the child’s death there was no longer any reason to fast, because he could not bring him back: “I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Did you know? Solomon was also given the name Jedidiah in this chapter. The name was given to him through the prophet Nathan, and its meaning is connected with the LORD’s love for him.
